title: IPC Section 302 — Punishment for Murder
text: IPC Section 302: Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. Murder is defined under Section 300 as culpable homicide amounting to murder when done with intention to cause death, or with intention of causing bodily injury likely to cause death.

title: IPC Section 354 — Assault or Criminal Force to Woman
text: IPC Section 354: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman, intending to outrage or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine.

title: IPC Section 406 — Punishment for Criminal Breach of Trust
text: IPC Section 406: Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Criminal breach of trust involves dishonest misappropriation or conversion of property entrusted to a person.

title: IPC Section 420 — Cheating and Dishonestly Inducing Delivery of Property
text: IPC Section 420: Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

title: IPC Section 498A — Husband or Relative of Husband Subjecting Woman to Cruelty
text: IPC Section 498A: Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine. Cruelty includes conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide, grave injury or danger to life, limb or health, or harassment to coerce her or her relatives to meet unlawful demands for property or valuable security.

title: IPC Section 379 — Punishment for Theft
text: IPC Section 379: Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Theft is defined in Section 378 as dishonest removal of moveable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent.

title: IPC Section 441 — Criminal Trespass
text: IPC Section 441: Whoever enters into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person in possession of such property, or having lawfully entered into or upon such property, unlawfully remains there with intent thereby to intimidate, insult or annoy any such person, or with intent to commit an offence, is said to commit criminal trespass.

title: CrPC Section 41 — Arrest by Police Without Warrant
text: CrPC Section 41 (as amended): A police officer may arrest without warrant any person who has been concerned in any cognizable offence. However, per the Supreme Court ruling in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014), police must apply their mind to whether arrest is necessary. Arrests in matrimonial disputes under Section 498A should not be mechanical. The officer must record reasons for not arresting.

title: CrPC Section 125 — Order for Maintenance of Wives, Children and Parents
text: CrPC Section 125: If any person having sufficient means neglects or refuses to maintain his wife unable to maintain herself, or his legitimate or illegitimate minor child unable to maintain itself, or his legitimate or illegitimate child (not being a married daughter) who has attained majority, where such child is by reason of any physical or mental abnormality or injury unable to maintain itself, or his father or mother unable to maintain themselves, a Magistrate of the first class may order such person to make a monthly allowance for the maintenance.

title: Article 14 — Right to Equality
text: Article 14 of the Constitution of India: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. This fundamental right prohibits class legislation but permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object sought.

title: Article 19 — Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression
text: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees to all citizens the right to freedom of speech and expression. This right can be restricted under Article 19(2) on grounds of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, or incitement to an offence. The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act as violating Article 19.

title: Article 21 — Protection of Life and Personal Liberty
text: Article 21: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. The Supreme Court has expansively interpreted Article 21 to include the right to privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017), right to livelihood, right to health, right to education, and right to a clean environment. Any deprivation must be just, fair and reasonable.

title: Article 32 — Right to Constitutional Remedies
text: Article 32 grants the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court can issue writs of Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari. Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 'the heart and soul of the Constitution'. Article 226 grants similar power to High Courts for both fundamental rights and other legal rights.

title: Industrial Disputes Act 1947 — Wrongful Termination
text: Under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, a workman employed for more than 240 days in a year cannot be terminated without prior notice and compensation. Section 25F requires: one month's notice or wages in lieu, retrenchment compensation at 15 days' wages for each completed year of service, and notice to appropriate government. Unfair labour practices are prohibited under Schedule V. A dismissed worker can approach the Labour Court within 3 years.

title: Minimum Wages Act 1948 — Wage Rights
text: Under the Minimum Wages Act 1948, every employer must pay minimum wages as fixed by the appropriate government. Failure to pay minimum wages is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 500 or both. Workers can file complaints with the Labour Commissioner. The Payment of Wages Act 1936 ensures wages are paid on time and without unauthorized deductions.

title: Transfer of Property Act 1882 — Property Rights
text: Under the Transfer of Property Act 1882, property can be transferred by sale, mortgage, lease, exchange, or gift. A sale deed must be in writing, signed, and registered for immovable property above Rs 100. Section 53A provides protection to a transferee in possession of property under part performance of contract. Encroachment on property can be addressed through a civil suit for injunction and possession under the Specific Relief Act.

title: Rent Control Laws — Tenant and Landlord Rights
text: Most Indian states have Rent Control Acts that protect tenants from arbitrary eviction and regulate rent. A landlord can evict a tenant for: non-payment of rent, subletting without permission, causing damage to property, or landlord's genuine personal use. Notice of 15 days to 3 months must be given depending on state law. Tenant can approach Rent Controller or Civil Court. Security deposit refund: landlord must return deposit within 30 days of vacating.

title: Consumer Protection Act 2019 — Consumer Rights
text: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 defines a consumer as any person who buys goods or avails services for personal use. A consumer can file a complaint for defective goods, deficient services, unfair trade practices, or misleading advertisements. District Consumer Commission handles claims up to Rs 1 crore, State Commission up to Rs 10 crore, and National Commission above that. Complaints can be filed within 2 years of cause of action. E-commerce platforms are also covered.

title: IT Act — Cyber Crime Provisions
text: The Information Technology Act 2000 (amended 2008) covers cyber crimes. Section 66 deals with computer-related offences. Section 66C addresses identity theft (imprisonment up to 3 years). Section 66D covers cheating by personation using computer (imprisonment up to 3 years). Section 67 penalizes publishing obscene material electronically. Section 43A mandates data protection by body corporates. Section 66A was struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015).

title: Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 — Anti-Dowry Law
text: The Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 prohibits giving or taking dowry. Section 3 punishes giving or taking dowry with imprisonment not less than 5 years and fine not less than Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry. Section 4 punishes demanding dowry with imprisonment not less than 6 months. Under Section 498A IPC, cruelty for dowry is punishable. Section 304B IPC (dowry death) carries minimum 7 years imprisonment. Women can approach National Commission for Women (NCW) for help.

title: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
text: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (PWDVA) provides civil remedies for domestic violence. The aggrieved woman can apply to a Magistrate for: Protection Order (preventing further violence), Residence Order (right to live in shared household), Monetary Relief (compensation for injuries, loss of earnings), Custody Order, and Compensation Order. A Protection Officer assists the victim. Violation of a Protection Order is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment up to 1 year. Emergency helpline: 181.

title: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 — Divorce and Marriage Rights
text: The Hindu Marriage Act 1955 governs marriages and divorces among Hindus. Grounds for divorce under Section 13 include: adultery, cruelty, desertion for 2 years, conversion to another religion, mental disorder, communicable disease, renunciation. Mutual consent divorce under Section 13B: parties can file jointly after 1 year of separation, with a 6-month cooling period (waivable by Supreme Court). Alimony (maintenance) under Section 25: court can order permanent alimony. Child custody under Section 26.

title: Vishaka Guidelines — Sexual Harassment at Workplace
text: In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), the Supreme Court laid down Vishaka Guidelines for prevention of sexual harassment at the workplace, later codified in the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013 (POSH Act). Every employer with 10+ employees must constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC). Workplace sexual harassment includes unwelcome physical contact, demands for sexual favours, sexually coloured remarks, showing pornography. Complaint must be filed within 3 months. Employer non-compliance carries fine up to Rs 50,000.

title: Right to Information Act 2005
text: The Right to Information Act 2005 (RTI) empowers every citizen to request information from public authorities. A Public Information Officer (PIO) must respond within 30 days (48 hours if life or liberty at stake). Fee: Rs 10 per application. If denied, appeal to First Appellate Authority within 30 days, then to Central/State Information Commission within 90 days. False information, obstruction of RTI: penalty up to Rs 25,000 on the PIO.

title: Negotiable Instruments Act Section 138 — Cheque Bounce
text: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds is a criminal offence. Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. Procedure: payee must send demand notice within 30 days of dishonour, drawer must pay within 15 days, then criminal complaint can be filed within 30 days. File complaint in Magistrate's Court of the area where payee's bank is located. Civil suit for recovery of amount can also be filed separately.

title: How to File an FIR — First Information Report
text: An FIR (First Information Report) is filed under Section 154 CrPC at the nearest police station for cognizable offences. Any person who knows about a cognizable offence can file an FIR. Police cannot refuse to register an FIR. If police refuse, approach the Superintendent of Police (SP) or file a private complaint under Section 200 CrPC before a Magistrate. After filing, you are entitled to a free copy. Online FIR can be filed in many states. Zero FIR can be filed at any police station regardless of jurisdiction.

title: Bail Provisions — Bailable and Non-Bailable Offences
text: Under CrPC, offences are classified as bailable (Schedule I, First Column) and non-bailable. For bailable offences, bail is a right. For non-bailable offences, bail is discretionary (Section 437 CrPC). Application for regular bail is made before the court where the case is pending. Anticipatory bail (Section 438) can be sought before arrest from Sessions Court or High Court. Supreme Court in Arnesh Kumar (2014) held that arrest should not be the norm for offences with 7 years or less sentence.

title: Free Legal Aid — Legal Services Authorities Act 1987
text: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 and Article 39A of the Constitution, free legal aid is available to: members of SC/ST, women, children, persons with disability, victims of trafficking, industrial workmen, persons in custody, persons with annual income below Rs 3 lakh (varies by state). Contact: District Legal Services Authority (DLSA), Taluk Legal Services Committee, State Legal Services Authority (SLSA). National helpline: 15100. Lok Adalats provide alternate dispute resolution and their awards are final and binding.

title: BNS Section 103 — Punishment for Murder
text: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 103: Replaces old IPC Section 302. Section 103(1) mandates that whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. Crucially, Section 103(2) introduces a brand new provision for mob lynching: where a group of five or more persons acts in concert to commit murder on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, or personal belief, each member shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life or a term not less than 7 years.

title: BNS Section 351 — Criminal Intimidation
text: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 351: Replaces old IPC Section 503/506. Whoever threatens another with any injury to their person, reputation, or property, or to anyone they are interested in, with intent to cause alarm or force them to do/omit an act, commits criminal intimidation. Basic offense carries up to 2 years imprisonment, or fine, or both. Under BNS 351(3), if the threat is to cause death, grievous hurt, or destruction of property by fire, the punishment extends up to 7 years imprisonment.

title: BNS Section 69 — Intercourse by Deceitful Means or False Promise of Marriage
text: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 69: An entirely new offense creating a clear line distinction from rape. It penalizes anyone who, by deceitful means or making a false promise of marriage without the intention of fulfilling it, marries or has sexual intercourse with a woman. Deceitful means include false promises of employment, promotion, inducement, or marrying after suppressing true identity. Punishable with imprisonment of either description up to 10 years and liability to a fine.

title: BNS Section 106 — Causing Death by Negligence (Hit and Run)
text: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 106: Replaces old IPC Section 304A. Section 106(1) states that causing death by any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide carries up to 5 years imprisonment. Crucially, Section 106(2) creates the strict 'Hit-and-Run' provision: if a person drives rashly, causes death, and escapes the scene without reporting it to a police officer or Magistrate soon after the incident, the punishment escalates up to 10 years imprisonment and a fine.

title: BNS Section 111 — Organized Crime
text: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 111: A landmark explicit inclusion defining organized crime. It covers any continuing unlawful activity (such as kidnapping, robbery, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offenses, cyber-crimes) committed by individuals acting singly or jointly as a member of an organized crime syndicate using violence, coercion, or intimidation to gain direct/indirect financial benefit. If it results in death, the punishment is death or life imprisonment with a minimum fine of Rs 5 lakh.

title: BNS Section 113 — Terrorist Act
text: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 113: Integrates anti-terror provisions explicitly into the general penal code. It defines a terrorist act as any act committed with intent to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or to strike terror in the people, by using bombs, firearms, hazardous materials, or cyber attacks. If the act results in death, the punishment is death or life imprisonment without parole.

title: BNSS Section 173 — Registration of FIR & Zero FIR Mandatory
text: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) Section 173: Replaces old CrPC Section 154. It modernizes the tracking of crimes by explicitly establishing 'Zero FIR'. A citizen can register a complaint at any police station across India, regardless of where the crime occurred. It mandates that electronic information (e-FIR) can be submitted, provided it is signed by the complainant within 3 days. For offenses carrying 3 to 7 years, it permits a preliminary inquiry within 14 days before registering an FIR.

title: BNSS Section 176 — Mandatory Forensic Investigation
text: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) Section 176: A structural upgrade making forensic evidence collection mandatory for any offense punishable with an imprisonment of 7 years or more. Forensic experts must visit the crime scene to gather evidence and video-record the process on a mobile device or electronic medium without tampering, ensuring the authenticity of the recovery chain.

title: BSA Section 57 — Electronic and Digital Records as Primary Evidence
text: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) Section 57: Completely overhauls old Indian Evidence Act rules. It elevates digital and electronic records to the status of primary evidence. If a digital record is produced directly from a proper computer output, server log, cloud storage, smartphone video, or encrypted chat application (such as WhatsApp or Signal logs), it is legally recognized as primary evidence without requiring the tedious secondary authentication parameters previously required.

title: BNS Section 49 — Community Service as Punishment
text: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 49: Introduces a reformative framework by defining 'Community Service' as an official form of criminal punishment for petty offenses. It targets minor infractions like public misconduct under the influence, defamation, small thefts under Rs 5,000 (if recovered), or trespassing. The court dictates non-custodial service beneficial to the local community, keeping non-violent first-time offenders out of congested prisons.

title: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007
text: Under this Act, senior citizens (aged 60+) who cannot maintain themselves from their own income/property have a legal right to apply to a dedicated Maintenance Tribunal. Children or legal heirs are obligated to provide a monthly allowance (up to Rs 10,000). Crucially, Section 23 states that if a senior citizen transferred property to an heir via gift/deed on the condition that they would receive basic care, and the heir refuses maintenance, the Tribunal can declare the property transfer completely void.

title: Commercial Courts Act 2015 — Mandatory Pre-Institution Mediation
text: The Commercial Courts Act mandates that any commercial dispute valued above Rs 3 lakh cannot file a regular civil suit directly unless urgent interim relief is sought. Under Section 12A, parties must first undergo Pre-Institution Mediation through the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) within a strict 3-month window. If a settlement is reached during mediation, it carries the exact same legal weight and enforceability as an official court decree.

title: POSH Act 2013 — Statutory Complaint Timelines and ICC Powers
text: Under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, a complaint must be submitted to the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) within 3 months of the incident. The ICC has the powers of a Civil Court to summon witnesses and examine evidence. The inquiry must be completed within 90 days. The employer is legally bound to implement the ICC’s recommendation within 60 days. False or malicious complaints are subject to disciplinary action under section 14.

title: RERA Act 2016 — Builder Delay and Refund Rights
text: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA) protects homebuyers from project delays. Under Section 18, if a builder fails to give possession of an apartment within the date specified in the agreement, the buyer has the absolute right to withdraw from the project and claim a full refund of the amount paid along with interest at prescribed penal rates. If the buyer chooses to stay in the project, the builder must pay monthly interest for every single month of delay until possession is handed over.

title: Maternity Benefit Amendment Act 2017 — Paid Leave Rights
text: The Maternity Benefit Act mandates that every woman employee who has worked for at least 80 days in the past 12 months is entitled to 26 weeks of fully paid maternity leave (up to 8 weeks can be taken prior to the expected delivery date). For women having 2 or more surviving children, the paid leave is capped at 12 weeks. Every establishment with 50 or more employees is legally required to provide an internal crèche facility within a specified distance, allowing 4 visits per day.

title: BNS Section 78 — Stalking (Physical and Cyber)
text: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 78: Replaces old IPC Section 354D. It targets cyber-stalking and harassment. Any man who monitors the use by a woman of the internet, email, or any other form of electronic communication, or follows a woman and contacts her repeatedly despite clear indications of disinterest, commits stalking. First conviction carries up to 3 years imprisonment and fine; a second or subsequent conviction carries up to 5 years imprisonment.

title: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 — Statutory Forfeiture Rules
text: Gratuity is a statutory terminal benefit for employees who complete 5 or more years of continuous service. Under Section 4(6), an employer can only forfeit gratuity under strict, narrow conditions: if the employee’s services were officially terminated for violent/riotous conduct, an act of moral turpitude, or causing willful damage/loss to the employer's property. Gratuity cannot be withheld or delayed simply because of a general resignation dispute or ongoing civil performance rows.

title: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 — Section 18 No Anticipatory Bail
text: This Act protects members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes from discrimination, humiliation, and violence. Offenses registered under this Act are strictly non-bailable. Section 18 explicitly bars the grant of Anticipatory Bail to an accused under Section 438 of the CrPC/BNSS. However, the Supreme Court in Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020) clarified that if a prima facie file check shows no basic case of atrocity exists, the court can exercise discretionary power to grant relief.

title: Copyright Act 1957 — Fair Use and Infringement
text: Under Section 51 of the Copyright Act, using copyrighted work without authorization constitutes infringement. However, Section 52 defines explicit 'Fair Dealings' exceptions that do not constitute an offense: private or personal use (including research), criticism or review of that work, reporting current events in newspapers/broadcasts, or educational teaching by a teacher in a classroom. Unauthorized commercial reproduction carries criminal liabilities including jail terms up to 3 years.

title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act Section 9 — Interim Relief
text: Section 9 allows a party to a commercial arbitration agreement to approach a Court directly to seek urgent interim protections before the arbitration tribunal is officially constituted or even during the ongoing arbitral proceedings. The court can order the freezing of bank accounts, secure the amount in dispute, appoint a receiver, or issue an injunction to prevent the sale or destruction of disputed properties.

title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 — Moratorium Protection
text: Under the IBC, once an application for corporate insolvency resolution is officially admitted by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) under Section 7 or Section 9, an automatic 'Moratorium' goes into effect under Section 14. This legally freezes all debt recovery actions, asset foreclosures, execution of decrees, or new lawsuits against the debtor company by any financial or operational creditors during the resolution period.

title: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 — Unlimited Third-Party Liability
text: Under Section 146 of the Motor Vehicles Act, driving an uninsured vehicle in a public place is a criminal offense. Crucially, the law establishes 'Unlimited Liability' for insurance companies concerning third-party bodily injury or death caused by an auto accident. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) calculates compensation structurally based on the victim's age, income capacity, and dependency factors, without any arbitrary maximum upper liability cap.

title: Medical Negligence Standards — Jacob Mathew Case
text: In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005), the Supreme Court established strict structural guardrails to protect doctors from malicious criminal prosecutions for negligence. To book a medical practitioner under criminal law (now BNS Negligence), the prosecution must establish a degree of 'gross negligence'—proving the doctor exhibited a complete disregard for safety. Before registering a criminal FIR, the police must source an independent medical opinion from a competent government panel doctor.

title: Equal Remuneration Act 1976 — Gender Pay Equality
text: This statute mandates that employers must pay equal remuneration to men and women workers for performing the 'same work or work of a similar nature'. Section 4 explicitly bars any reduction in salary scales to clear up anomalies. Section 5 prohibits employers from discriminating against women during regular recruitment processes, promotions, training, or structural transfers, except where the employment of women in specific night shifts is legally barred by separate factory safety statutes.

title: Juvenile Justice Act 2015 — Trial of Minors as Adults
text: Under Section 15 of the JJ Act, if a juvenile between the ages of 16 and 18 years commits a 'heinous offense' (defined as a crime carrying a statutory minimum punishment of 7 years or more imprisonment, such as murder or rape), the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) must conduct a mandatory preliminary assessment regarding their mental and physical capacity to commit the crime and understand its consequences. Based on this, the case can be transferred to a regular Children's Court to try them as an adult.

title: Negotiable Instruments Act Section 143A — Interim Compensation
text: To prevent accused drawers from deliberately dragging out litigation, Section 143A allows the Magistrate court to order the drawer of a bounced cheque to pay up to 20% of the total face value of the cheque as 'Interim Compensation' to the complainant. This amount must be deposited within 60 days of the framing of formal charges. If the accused is later completely acquitted at the trial's conclusion, the complainant is ordered to refund the interim money back with bank interest.

title: Passports Act 1967 — Criminal Case Restrictions
text: Under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, the Passport Authority has the administrative power to impound or revoke a passport if a criminal case is pending against the holder in an Indian court, or if a warrant for their arrest has been issued. A citizen facing an ongoing criminal trial cannot travel abroad unless they secure an explicit, conditional 'No Objection Certificate' (NOC) and travel authorization order directly from the specific magistrate judge handling their trial.

title: Hindu Succession Amendment Act 2005 — Daughter's Property Rights
text: A landmark amendment to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act 1956. It explicitly establishes that in a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF), a daughter becomes a 'coparcener' (joint legal heir) by birth, carrying the exact same ancestral property rights and liabilities as a son. The Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) confirmed this operates retroactively: the daughter is entitled to her ancestral coparcenary share even if her father had passed away before the amendment was signed.

title: Limitation Act 1963 — Statutory Debt Recovery Window
text: The Limitation Act sets rigid timelines for filing lawsuits. Under the Schedule to the Act, a civil suit for the recovery of a monetary debt, unpaid invoices, or a broken contract loan must be filed within a strict period of 3 years. This clock starts ticking exactly from the date the debt debt became due or when the breach of contract occurred. If the creditor fails to initiate legal actions within this 3-year window, the debt becomes legally time-barred and unenforceable.

title: Specific Relief Amendment Act 2018 — Specific Performance Mandate
text: The 2018 amendment structurally changed Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act 1963. Previously, courts treated ordering the specific performance of a broken contract as a highly discretionary power, usually choosing to grant monetary damages instead. The amendment removes court discretion: it is now mandatory for civil courts to order the literal performance of a contract (e.g., executing a property sale deed) unless the case explicitly falls under narrow statutory disqualifications.
